doctrine:
**Whether an injury is fatal is a question of fact. Absent testimony from the attending physician that the injury would have caused the victim's death without timely medical assistance, the Court cannot presume that it is fatal, even if the medico-legal certificate shows that vital organs were involved or that significant blood loss occurred, "since what may be fatal for one person may not be fatal for another."** In a prosecution for frustrated homicide, the victim's wounds must be proven beyond reasonable doubt to be fatal through the testimony of the physician who attended to them. A medical certificate is merely the opinion of one who must first be established as an expert, and the defense must be able to cross-examine its author; a stipulation on the certificate's existence is not enough. The doubt on the character of the wounds is resolved in favor of the accused, so the crime is only **attempted homicide** (reiterating *Etino v. People* and *Oliveros v. People*).

Circumstantial evidence suffices to convict under **Rule 133, Section 4** when (a) there is more than one circumstance, (b) the facts from which the inferences are derived are proven, and (c) the combination of all the circumstances produces a conviction beyond reasonable doubt. The circumstances must form an unbroken chain pointing to the accused, to the exclusion of all others, as the guilty person (reiterated).

Voluntary surrender is not appreciated when the accused gives himself up only after the police come to his house, tell his family he is a suspect, and ask his parents to surrender him; the surrender must be spontaneous. Treachery proven at trial but not alleged in the Information cannot qualify the crime to murder, but it supports an award of exemplary damages; the Court reiterated *People v. Solar*'s reminder to prosecutors to allege attendant circumstances with particularity.
facts:
Ian Solis and the minors XXX (his brother), YYY and ZZZ were charged with frustrated homicide (Criminal Case No. 2017-0215-D) for stabbing Jun Ferriol around 1:30 a.m. of March 3, 2017 in Pangasinan, with intent to kill and in conspiracy, the victim surviving because of timely medical attendance. They were also charged with theft (Criminal Case No. 2017-0216-D). Ian, XXX and YYY were acquitted of theft. ZZZ escaped during the proceedings; when he surrendered, Jun executed an affidavit of desistance and the case against him was dismissed.

Ian, a friend of Jun for two years, came to Jun's house with his three companions around 10:30 p.m. of March 2, 2017. They drank brandy and watched a movie. Jun went to sleep and told them to lock the door when they left. He woke up to a pair of scissors in his right side; someone choked him while others covered his mouth and held his hands and feet. The room was dim, so he did not see his attackers. He played dead until they left, then went to his mother's house and was operated on at the Medical City Pangasinan. At the scene, the police found a blood-stained pair of scissors and a mobile phone bearing a picture of a man whom neighbors identified as Ian. Tricycle driver Noel Garcia said that around 2:30 a.m. he drove four teenagers who were rushing and seemed afraid of something; one carried a black bag, and another wore a blood-stained shirt. The police went to Ian's house, told his parents that Ian was a suspect, and asked them to surrender him; Ian then surrendered. Around 7:20 a.m., Garcia identified the four at the police station, naming Ian as the one still wearing the bloodied shirt. The accused claimed they left Jun's house at 11:00 p.m. and never returned.

The existence of the medico-legal certificate was stipulated; the attending physician did not testify. The certificate showed stab wounds that injured Jun's liver, colon and kidney, with about 400 ml of blood in the abdominal cavity. The hospital's total charges were PHP 288,993.65, but the final amount due after discounts was PHP 201,478.65.

The RTC convicted Ian, XXX and YYY of frustrated homicide, appreciated voluntary surrender for Ian, and awarded actual damages of PHP 282,993.65 and moral damages of PHP 20,000.00. The CA affirmed with modification, increasing the penalty and adding PHP 30,000.00 civil indemnity and PHP 10,000.00 more in moral damages. Ian's motion for reconsideration was denied. In his Rule 45 petition, Ian argued that the circumstantial evidence did not prove his identity as one of the assailants.
issues: Whether the prosecution proved, through circumstantial evidence, that Ian was one of the persons who stabbed Jun.
Whether the crime committed was frustrated homicide, when the fatal character of the wounds was shown only by a medico-legal certificate whose author did not testify.
Whether Ian is entitled to the mitigating circumstance of voluntary surrender.
Whether the civil liabilities were correctly awarded.
ruling:
**1. Yes, Ian's identity was proven by circumstantial evidence.** The petition raised questions of fact beyond Rule 45, but even on review the lower courts were correct. Direct evidence is not required to convict, and its probative value is generally not superior to circumstantial evidence. The CA relied on eight circumstances: Ian and his companions were at the scene before the attack; they drank until Jun slept ahead of them; Jun woke to a stab from scissors; several persons held him while one stabbed him; contrary to their claim of leaving at 11:00 p.m., Garcia drove them at around 2:30 a.m., close to when the crime was reported; they were in a hurry; one passenger wore a bloodstained shirt; and Ian's phone was found at the scene. Each was proven by Ian's admission, Jun's testimony, Garcia's testimony or the police testimony, and together they were consistent with guilt and inconsistent with innocence. Garcia identified Ian about five hours later as the one in the bloodied shirt. As in *People v. Casitas*, where the accused was seen leaving the victim's house in blood-soaked clothes, **the fact that only Ian wore a bloodied shirt led to the conclusion that he was the one who stabbed Jun, to the exclusion of his companions or any other person.** Non-presentation of the shirt was not fatal, since it was merely corroborative. The RTC's credibility findings, affirmed by the CA, were binding.

**2. No, only attempted homicide was proven.** The elements of frustrated homicide are: (1) intent to kill, as shown by the use of a deadly weapon; (2) the victim sustained fatal wounds but did not die because of timely medical assistance; and (3) no qualifying circumstance for murder. Intent to kill was shown by the use of scissors and the number and location of the wounds. But the lower courts proved the second element only by the medico-legal certificate, whose existence was stipulated without the attending physician's testimony. Unlike in rape, where medical examination is not indispensable, in frustrated homicide the wounds must be "proven beyond reasonable doubt to be fatal through the testimony of the physician who attended to said fatal wounds." Citing *Etino*, "where there is nothing in the evidence to show that the wound would be fatal if not medically attended to, the character of the wound is doubtful," and the doubt is resolved in favor of the accused. **Ian could be held liable only for attempted homicide; the Court "cannot presume" the wounds fatal even if vital organs were involved or significant blood loss occurred.**

**3. No.** Voluntary surrender requires that (1) the accused was not arrested, (2) he surrendered to a person in authority or an agent, and (3) the surrender was voluntary, showing spontaneity and an intent to surrender unconditionally. Ian surrendered only when the police were already at his house and had told him and his family that he was a suspect, and the police even had to implore his parents to surrender him. **Voluntary surrender is not appreciated when the authorities' presence in the accused's house has already precluded his escape.**

**4. Modified.** For attempted homicide, civil indemnity and moral damages are PHP 20,000.00 each (*People v. Jugueta*). Because an aggravating circumstance was proven at trial though not alleged in the Information, exemplary damages of PHP 20,000.00 were also awarded: Jun was stabbed while asleep and unable to defend himself, which was treachery and would have qualified the crime to attempted murder had the Information alleged the ultimate facts constituting it. Actual damages were reduced to PHP 201,478.65, the final hospital bill after discounts and subsidies, since a party may recover only the pecuniary loss duly proven. The Court reiterated *People v. Solar* in urging prosecutors to state in the Information, with sufficient particularity, the qualifying and aggravating circumstances.
disposition: Petition DENIED. The CA Decision of July 10, 2020 and Resolution of January 20, 2021 in CA-G.R. CR No. 41501 were AFFIRMED with MODIFICATION. Ian Solis y Aquino was found GUILTY beyond reasonable doubt of attempted homicide and sentenced to an indeterminate penalty of six months of arresto mayor, as minimum, to four years and two months of prisión correccional, as maximum. He was ordered to pay Jun actual damages of PHP 201,478.65, and civil indemnity, moral damages and exemplary damages of PHP 20,000.00 each, all with 6% interest per annum from finality of the Decision until fully paid.

bar_questions.q: Marco stabbed Paolo several times in the abdomen with a kitchen knife. Paolo was rushed to the hospital and survived after emergency surgery. Marco was charged with frustrated homicide. At pre-trial, the parties stipulated on the existence of the medico-legal certificate, which stated that Paolo suffered penetrating stab wounds that lacerated his liver, with about 500 ml of blood loss. The attending surgeon was never presented. The prosecution argues that a lacerated liver and heavy blood loss are obviously fatal. If Marco's identity and intent to kill are proven, of what crime should he be convicted?

alac.answer: Marco should be convicted only of attempted homicide, not frustrated homicide.
alac.legal_basis: Frustrated homicide requires (1) intent to kill, (2) fatal wounds that did not cause death because of timely medical assistance, and (3) no qualifying circumstance for murder. Whether an injury is fatal is a question of fact. In a prosecution for frustrated homicide, the wounds must be proven beyond reasonable doubt to be fatal through the testimony of the attending physician; absent such testimony, the Court cannot presume the wounds fatal even if the medico-legal certificate shows that vital organs were involved or that significant blood loss occurred, since what may be fatal for one person may not be fatal for another. Doubt on the character of the wounds is resolved in favor of the accused. (Solis v. People, G.R. No. 255485, November 26, 2025, reiterating Etino v. People)
alac.application: Intent to kill is shown by the use of a knife and the location of the wounds. But the only proof that the wounds were fatal is the medico-legal certificate, whose existence alone was stipulated. Without the surgeon's testimony that Paolo would have died without timely medical help, and without the chance for the defense to cross-examine the author of the certificate, the fatal character of the wounds is doubtful. The involvement of the liver and the 500 ml blood loss do not allow the court to presume that the wounds were fatal.
alac.conclusion: With the second element of frustrated homicide not proven, Marco is guilty only of attempted homicide.

bar_questions.q: Same facts as in the previous question, except that the attending surgeon testified in court. She explained her qualifications, identified the medico-legal certificate, and stated that Paolo's liver wounds would have caused his death from internal bleeding within hours had he not undergone emergency surgery. The defense cross-examined her but did not shake her testimony. Of what crime should Marco be convicted?

alac.answer: Marco should be convicted of frustrated homicide.
alac.legal_basis: The second element of frustrated homicide, that the victim sustained fatal wounds but did not die because of timely medical assistance, must be proven beyond reasonable doubt through the testimony of the physician who attended to the wounds. A medical certificate gains weight when the doctor who issued it is presented to establish his or her qualifications and is subjected to cross-examination. (Solis v. People, G.R. No. 255485, November 26, 2025)
alac.application: Unlike in Solis, the prosecution here presented the attending surgeon, who established her qualifications and testified that the wounds would have caused Paolo's death without the emergency surgery. Her testimony was tested by cross-examination. This proves that the wounds were fatal and that Paolo survived only because of timely medical assistance. Since intent to kill is shown by the use of a knife and the nature and location of the wounds, and no qualifying circumstance is alleged, all elements of frustrated homicide are present.
alac.conclusion: With the fatal character of the wounds proven by the attending physician, Marco is guilty of frustrated homicide.

bar_questions.q: Lito stabbed Dino while Dino was fast asleep in his room. Dino survived. The Information charged Lito with attempted homicide and did not allege any qualifying or aggravating circumstance. At trial, the prosecution clearly proved that Dino was asleep and unable to defend himself when he was stabbed. (a) May Lito be convicted of attempted murder? (b) Does the proven circumstance have any effect on Lito's civil liability?

alac.answer: (a) No. Lito may be convicted only of attempted homicide. (b) Yes. Exemplary damages may be awarded.
alac.legal_basis: Stabbing a sleeping victim who is not in a position to defend himself constitutes treachery, which qualifies homicide to murder. However, qualifying and aggravating circumstances must be alleged in the Information with the ultimate facts constituting them (Rule 110, Secs. 8 and 9); otherwise they cannot qualify the crime or raise the penalty. In Solis v. People (G.R. No. 255485, November 26, 2025), treachery was proven but not alleged, so it could not qualify the crime to attempted murder; but because an aggravating circumstance was proven at trial although not alleged in the Information, the Court awarded exemplary damages of PHP 20,000.00, in addition to civil indemnity and moral damages of PHP 20,000.00 each for attempted homicide (citing People v. Jugueta), and reiterated People v. Solar's reminder to prosecutors.
alac.application: (a) Treachery was proven, but since the Information did not allege it, Lito cannot be convicted of attempted murder; doing so would violate his right to be informed of the nature and cause of the accusation. He is liable only for attempted homicide, the crime charged. (b) The proven treachery, though it cannot affect the crime or the penalty, justifies the award of exemplary damages, on top of civil indemnity and moral damages.
alac.conclusion: Lito is guilty only of attempted homicide, but the proven treachery entitles Dino to exemplary damages.

notes: XXX, YYY and ZZZ are minors whose names were replaced with fictitious initials under RA 9344; the victim's surname is also spelled "Ferreol" in parts of the record. The RTC also convicted XXX and YYY, but only Ian's petition was before the Court. The Decision says the RTC awarded actual damages of PHP 282,993.65 while the CA "arrived at PHP 288,993.65" (the total hospital charges) but upheld the RTC award; both were reduced to PHP 201,478.65. The Decision states that the medical findings showed "seven stab wounds"; the intraoperative findings it quotes also list non-penetrating wounds and abrasions. The penalty in the disposition is stated as the fallo reads; the 2027 Bar does not ask for computation of penalty periods.
